questions.prompt: You get an email that looks like it's from Microsoft 365, warning your password expires in 2 hours. The link goes to 'microsoft0nline-login.com'. What do you do?
options: Click the link and reset it now, since losing access for a day or two would stall your work
Reply to the sender and ask them to confirm the request is legitimate before acting
Leave the link alone, sign in at portal.office.com yourself, and report the email to IT
Forward it to a coworker to see whether they got the same warning about their password
questions.explanation: The domain 'microsoft0nline-login.com' is not a real Microsoft domain (note the zero instead of 'o', and the extra hyphenated words), a classic lookalike-domain trick. Urgency plus a mismatched URL is the core phishing pattern. Always navigate to sensitive sites directly rather than through emailed links, and report suspicious emails to IT/security.

questions.prompt: An email claiming to be from your HR department asks you to 'review and confirm' updated benefits info by clicking a button. The sender address is hr-benefits@company-hr-portal.net, not your company's actual domain.
options: Ask HR about it using a channel you already use, like the HR portal, before clicking
Click through, since benefits updates are routine and the message uses HR's usual tone
Open the button in an incognito window so nothing from the page sticks to your account
Forward it to your personal email and deal with it at home, away from the work network
questions.explanation: A mismatched sending domain is one of the strongest phishing indicators, even when the content looks plausible. Incognito mode does not protect you from credential theft or malware. The safe move is verifying through a separate, known-good channel (like Slack, an internal HR system, or calling HR) before interacting with the email at all.

questions.prompt: You receive a shared 'invoice' via a Google Docs link from an unfamiliar sender, with the subject 'URGENT: Overdue Payment Attached'. What's the safest action?
options: Open the doc, since Google hosts it and Google scans shared files for malware anyway
Report it as phishing and delete it, so nobody opens the link to see what's inside
Open the link to see what it is, but close it right away if it asks you to sign in
Reply to the sender and ask which invoice this is, so you can check it with finance
questions.explanation: Attackers frequently abuse legitimate platforms like Google Docs to host phishing pages or credential-harvesting forms, since the link itself passes spam filters. An urgent, unexpected invoice from an unknown sender is a red flag regardless of what platform hosts it. Report and delete rather than investigating it yourself.

questions.prompt: You get a phone call from someone claiming to be 'IT Support' saying your laptop is sending out malware and they need your VPN credentials immediately to stop it. What should you do?
options: Give them the VPN login, since IT needs to stop the malware before it spreads further
Decline to answer and ask them to email the request, so you have it in writing first
Hang up and call the IT help desk on the number listed on the company intranet instead
Give them a slightly wrong password to see how they react and whether they're real
questions.explanation: Legitimate IT departments will never ask for your password or credentials over an unsolicited phone call. The pressure and urgency are manipulation tactics. Always hang up and independently verify through a number or channel you already know is real, never one the caller provides.

questions.prompt: A caller says they're from your bank's fraud department and asks you to 'confirm your identity' by reading back a one-time passcode that was just texted to you.
options: Read the code back, since it's your own bank checking that you really are you
Ask them to text or email a fresh code first, so you know the code is current
Refuse, hang up, and call your bank yourself on the number printed on your card
Read only the last two digits, so they can match it without getting the whole code
questions.explanation: A real bank never needs you to read back a one-time passcode. That code exists specifically to prove a transaction request came from you, and a scammer asking for it is trying to authorize something in your name. Hang up and call the number printed on your card or statement, not one given by the caller.

questions.prompt: Someone calls claiming to be a vendor's tech support, referencing your company by name and asking you to install a 'remote access tool' to fix a ticket you don't remember opening.
options: Decline, hang up, and ask your IT team or vendor manager whether the ticket is real
Install it, since they know your company's name or details only a real vendor would know
Install it, but keep watching your screen so you can stop them if anything looks off
Ask a coworker if they opened the ticket, and if so, go ahead and install the tool
questions.explanation: Knowing your company's name is trivial for an attacker to find (LinkedIn, your own website, prior data breaches) and isn't proof of legitimacy. Unsolicited requests to install remote-access software are a classic vector for full system compromise. Verify independently through your actual vendor contact or IT team before granting any remote access.

questions.prompt: You get a text: 'Your package could not be delivered. Update your address here: [shortened link]'. You weren't expecting a package.
options: Delete it, and if you're curious, check the carrier's official app to see for sure
Tap the link just to see, since a delivery update doesn't ask for anything sensitive
Reply STOP to unsubscribe, so you don't keep getting these delivery notifications
Forward it to a friend to see if they got the same text before you do anything
questions.explanation: Shortened links hide the real destination, and unexpected delivery texts are one of the most common smishing lures. Replying 'STOP' can confirm to scammers that your number is active, inviting more attempts. If you want to check, go directly to the carrier's real app or site instead of the link.

questions.prompt: A text appears to come from your company's payroll system: 'Your direct deposit failed. Update your bank info now: [link]'.
options: Update it quickly through the link, so your next paycheck isn't held up by the error
Text back asking which account failed, so you know which bank details to update
Open the link to look at the page, but close it before entering any bank details
Contact HR or payroll using the usual internal channel before clicking anything
questions.explanation: Payroll and direct-deposit changes are a high-value target for attackers because a successful one redirects your actual paycheck. Legitimate payroll issues are handled through your company's real HR system, not an unsolicited text link. Always verify through a separate, trusted channel first.

questions.prompt: You receive a text claiming to be a 2FA code request you didn't initiate, followed by a second text saying 'If this wasn't you, click here to secure your account.'
options: Tap the link right away to lock down the account, since someone is trying to get in
Ignore both texts, since no code was entered anyway and nothing has happened yet
Reply to the text and ask who is trying to log in, so you know who's behind it
Skip the link, log in to the real service on your own, and change your password there
questions.explanation: This is a manipulation technique: the first text creates alarm, and the second offers a 'helpful' link that's actually the actual phishing payload. The safe move is never following links from unsolicited security texts. Go directly to the real service yourself if you want to check or change anything.

questions.prompt: Someone calls the front desk claiming to be a 'new contractor' who forgot their badge and needs someone to let them into the server room, name-dropping your IT manager.
options: Let them in, since they know the IT manager's name and seem to know the building well
Ask them to wait outside for someone official, but let them leave their bag inside
Give them directions to the server room and let them find their own way from there
Politely decline, then check their identity and access with the named manager before entry
questions.explanation: Name-dropping a real employee is a common pretexting tactic to build false trust, since the name may have been found on LinkedIn or a company directory. Physical access to sensitive areas should always be verified directly with the referenced person before granting entry, regardless of how confident or knowledgeable the requester sounds.

questions.prompt: An email from someone claiming to be a 'new auditor' asks you to send over a spreadsheet of employee usernames and department codes 'for a compliance review'.
options: Send it, since compliance reviews are routine and the email sounds professional
Send a smaller portion of the data first, and send the rest if they're legitimate
Decline for now and ask them to fill in an internal request form, then send it once it's back
Ask the compliance team to confirm that the auditor and the review are both real
questions.explanation: Attackers often invent a plausible-sounding role (auditor, new hire, vendor rep) to justify a data request that would otherwise seem suspicious. Any request for internal data, especially usernames or org structure info that could enable further attacks, should be verified through a known internal contact before being fulfilled.

questions.prompt: A caller claiming to be from your company's insurance provider asks to 'confirm' your full name, date of birth, and SSN to 'update records' after a supposed system migration.
options: Confirm the details, since the insurer already has all this data on file anyway
Don't confirm anything; call your insurer back on the number on your policy documents
Give a partial answer, like just your birth year, so nothing complete is shared
Ask them to mail or email a written request, and confirm the details once it arrives
questions.explanation: Even though your real insurer does have this data, that's exactly why it's a common pretext: attackers exploit the fact that the ask sounds routine. Never confirm sensitive personal identifiers to an inbound caller; call back using a number from an official document you already have, not one the caller gives you.

questions.prompt: You badge into a secure office entrance and someone behind you, carrying a large box and no visible badge, asks you to hold the door.
options: Hold the door, since it would be rude not to help someone carrying a heavy box
Politely ask them to badge in, or point them to the front desk so they can be signed in
Hold the door, but keep an eye on where they go once they're inside the office
Ask who they're visiting, and hold the door if the name they give sounds right
questions.explanation: This is a classic tailgating setup: carrying something bulky is a common excuse to get someone else to open a secured door. Politeness should never override access control; the appropriate response is directing them to badge in or check in at the front desk, not personally vouching for their entry.

questions.prompt: A person in a delivery uniform tries to follow you through a badge-access door into a restricted area, saying they 'do this delivery every week.'
options: Let them through, since they clearly know the routine and do this every week
Let them in, but tell them to go straight to the drop-off point and not wander
Ask them to check in at the front desk or loading dock, not through the employee door
Ask to see their delivery paperwork or ID, and let them in if everything matches up
questions.explanation: A uniform and familiarity with a routine are easy to fake or observe, and don't verify legitimate access. Deliveries should go through a designated, monitored entrance (loading dock, front desk) rather than employee-only badge doors, regardless of how routine the person makes it sound.

questions.prompt: You're heading into a restricted lab area and a coworker you don't recognize, wearing a lanyard with no visible badge photo, walks in right behind you without scanning.
options: Assume it's fine, since they're wearing a company lanyard and look like they belong
Ask them to badge in separately, and tell security if they won't do it themselves
Let it go, since confronting a coworker you don't know would be really awkward
Ask what department they're from, and let it go if the answer sounds reasonable
questions.explanation: A lanyard alone isn't proof of authorization, since badges can be visually similar or intentionally vague. Restricted areas rely on every individual badging in themselves; politely but firmly asking them to do so (or escalating to security if they refuse) is the correct response, even though it can feel socially uncomfortable.

questions.prompt: You receive an email that appears to be from your CEO, sent from their real-looking name but a slightly different email domain, asking you to urgently purchase $2,000 in gift cards for a 'client gift' and send the codes right away.
options: Buy the gift cards quickly, because the CEO marked it urgent and the client can't wait
Reply asking which client the gift is for, so you can pick the right gift cards
Buy a smaller amount first to test whether it's real before buying the rest
Confirm with the CEO by phone on a known number, or in person, before doing anything
questions.explanation: Gift card requests are one of the most common BEC (Business Email Compromise) patterns, precisely because gift card codes are instantly usable and untraceable, unlike a wire transfer. Urgency plus an unusual payment method from a senior exec is a major red flag. Always verify out-of-band before acting.

questions.prompt: An email from your company's 'CFO' asks you to change the bank account on file for a longtime vendor, citing a 'recent account switch,' with instructions to update it before the next invoice is paid.
options: Update it, since changing a vendor's bank details is routine admin work for finance
Update it, but flag the next invoice for review after it has been paid out
Check with the CFO over email once more, so you have their approval in writing
Call the vendor on contact details you already had on file before changing anything
questions.explanation: Vendor bank-detail change requests are a textbook BEC tactic for redirecting a legitimate, expected payment to an attacker-controlled account. Confirming over email again doesn't help if the CFO's account itself is compromised. Always verify banking changes directly with the vendor via a previously established phone number, not new details provided in the request itself.

questions.prompt: You get a message on Slack, seemingly from your manager, asking you to process an 'urgent wire transfer' before end of day for a deal that 'can't wait for the usual approval process.'
options: Process it, since Slack feels more secure than email and it came from your manager
Ask a coworker to help you push it through faster, so the deal isn't held up today
Follow the normal approval process anyway, and confirm with your manager by phone first
Process half the amount now to reduce the risk, and the rest once it's approved
questions.explanation: Chat platforms like Slack can also be spoofed or accessed via a compromised account, so the platform itself isn't a safety guarantee. Requests to skip established approval processes, especially involving money, are a major red flag regardless of who appears to be asking. Verify through a separate channel every time.

questions.prompt: You find a USB drive labeled 'Q4 Salary Review: Confidential' in the office parking lot. What should you do?
options: Plug it in to see whose it is, so you can get it back to the right person quickly
Hand it to the security team without plugging it into any computer, even one at home
Plug it into a personal laptop or an old spare one to keep it off the work network entirely
Leave it where you found it, since whoever dropped it will probably come back
questions.explanation: This is a classic 'USB drop' attack: an enticing label is used to bait curiosity, and plugging it in (even on a personal device) can trigger malware. The correct response is handing it to IT/security so it can be safely inspected, without ever connecting it to any computer yourself.

questions.prompt: A flyer at a coffee shop near your office has a QR code for '20% off your next order.' Scanning it opens a page asking you to log in with your work email to 'verify eligibility.'
options: Don't log in, since a coffee discount has no reason to need your work credentials
Log in, since it's just a local discount and a coffee shop can't do much with it
Sign in through your personal email instead, so your work account is never at risk
Scan it again, or try a different phone, to check the same page comes up before logging in
questions.explanation: This is 'quishing' (QR code phishing): a legitimate-looking physical flyer leading to a credential-harvesting page. A real discount offer has no legitimate reason to require your work login. Any QR code requesting credentials, especially work ones, in an unrelated context should be treated as suspicious.

questions.prompt: A vendor at a conference hands you a free USB-powered phone charger/fan branded with their logo. Back at the office, you want to charge your phone with it.
options: Plug it into your work laptop, since it's only a charger and can't hold any files
Plug it into a coworker's computer instead, so your own laptop stays protected
Charge from a wall outlet or through a USB data blocker, not a computer's port
Use it anywhere, since it came from a real company at a legitimate conference
questions.explanation: Free branded USB gadgets are a known vector for 'juice jacking' or hidden malicious firmware, even from seemingly legitimate vendors (promotional items are sometimes manufactured by third parties with unknown supply-chain integrity). Charging through a wall outlet or a data-blocker avoids exposing your computer's USB data lines entirely.

questions.prompt: You get a phone call that sounds exactly like your company's CEO, urgently asking you to approve a wire transfer, using their real speech patterns and tone. Your caller ID even shows their name.
options: Hang up and reach the CEO on a channel you already use, like their known number
Approve it, since the voice, the tone, and the caller ID all match the real CEO
Ask the caller to repeat the request slowly or answer a question only the CEO would know
Approve a smaller amount now as a compromise, and the rest after checking it
questions.explanation: AI voice cloning can now convincingly mimic a real person's voice from just a few seconds of public audio (interviews, videos, podcasts), and caller ID can be spoofed. Voice and caller ID matching is no longer reliable proof of identity for high-stakes requests. Always verify financial or sensitive requests through a separate, already-trusted channel.

questions.prompt: A family member calls sounding distressed, claiming to be in trouble and urgently needing money sent via a payment app, and the voice sounds just like them.
options: Send the money right away, since they sound genuinely scared and need help now
Ask them a question only they would know, and send the money if they get it right
Hang up and call them back on the number you have saved, before sending anything at all
Send a smaller amount to help for now, and check what's going on after that
questions.explanation: AI voice cloning scams increasingly target personal relationships, not just workplaces, using short audio clips scraped from social media. Even answering a 'security question' on the same call doesn't help if the attacker is also using real-time AI voice conversion or has done research. Hanging up and calling back on a known number is the only reliable verification.

questions.prompt: During a video call, a colleague's video and voice look and sound normal, but they suddenly ask you to share your screen and read out a one-time passcode you're about to receive.
options: Read it out, since you can see and hear them clearly and it's clearly your colleague
Decline, end the call, and reach them another way, since video can be faked
Read out only part of the code, so they can't use it even if something is off
Decline for now, ask why they need it, and read it out if the reason makes good sense
questions.explanation: Real-time deepfake video and voice tools have advanced enough to convincingly impersonate someone in a live call. No legitimate colleague needs you to read a one-time passcode to them under any circumstance. This is one of the clearest signals of an attack, regardless of how convincing the call appears.

questions.prompt: You step away from your desk for a quick coffee break, leaving your laptop unlocked and logged in to internal systems.
options: Leave it, since it's a quick break and everyone around you is a coworker anyway
Close the laptop lid instead of locking it, since that hides the screen just as well
Lock your screen every time you step away, even if it's just for a minute or two
Turn the monitor off so nobody walking past can see what's on your screen
questions.explanation: An unlocked, logged-in workstation is a serious exposure even for 'just a minute', since anyone passing by (employee, visitor, or an attacker who tailgated in) has full access to your accounts and data. Closing the lid or turning off the monitor doesn't prevent access; locking the screen (Win+L / Cmd+Ctrl+Q) takes seconds and should be automatic.

questions.prompt: You're finishing sensitive documents at your desk and need to leave for the day. What's the correct way to handle the printed pages?
options: Shred them before you leave, using the secure confidential bin if there's no shredder
Leave them on your desk, since the office is locked overnight and it's just a night
Put them in the regular recycling bin, since recycling gets collected every night
Stack them neatly in an unlocked drawer so they're ready for you in the morning
questions.explanation: Cleaning crews, other tenants, or anyone with after-hours access could see sensitive documents left on a desk or thrown in regular recycling ('dumpster diving' is a real, low-tech data theft method). Confidential material should always go through a secure shredding/disposal process, not general trash or recycling.

questions.prompt: While working at a coffee shop, you need to step away briefly to use the restroom. Your laptop is open with your work email visible.
options: Ask the person at the next table to keep an eye on it, since it's only a few minutes
Lock the screen and take the laptop with you, or pack it away in your bag entirely
Just close the lid and leave it there, since sleep mode locks the screen anyway
Leave it, since people in a coffee shop generally don't touch other people's things
questions.explanation: Asking a stranger to 'watch' a device doesn't protect against theft or shoulder-surfing, and closing the lid can leave it in a resumable sleep state depending on settings. In public spaces, taking sensitive devices with you (or packing them away, screen locked) is the only reliable option, both against theft and against visible data on the screen.

questions.prompt: You start getting a rapid series of push-notification login approval requests on your phone that you didn't initiate, one after another, late at night.
options: Approve one to make the notifications stop, so you can finally get back to sleep
Ignore them and go back to sleep, since they'll stop on their own eventually
Approve one, since it might just be a delayed login from your laptop or phone earlier
Deny all of them, change your password right away, and report it to IT
questions.explanation: This is an 'MFA fatigue' or 'push bombing' attack: an attacker who already has your password spams approval requests hoping you'll approve one out of annoyance or confusion. Every request should be denied, and the incident reported immediately, since it confirms your password is already compromised even though MFA hasn't been bypassed yet.

questions.prompt: You receive one unexpected MFA push notification while you're not actively logging into anything. It's just a single request, not a flood.
options: Approve it, since it's only one request and probably just a random glitch
Ignore it and do nothing, because a single request isn't worth changing a password over
Deny it and change your password, since an unexpected request means it's known
Approve it, then keep an eye on your account for anything unusual afterward
questions.explanation: Even a single unrequested MFA prompt means someone else already has your username and password and is one tap away from getting in. It doesn't need to be a flood to be a real attack. Treat any unexpected authentication request as a sign of compromise: deny it and change your password immediately.

questions.prompt: After denying several unexpected MFA push requests, you get a call from someone claiming to be 'IT' saying they see the failed logins and need you to approve the next one so they can 'verify your account is secure.'
options: Approve the next one, since it's IT asking and they can see the failed logins
Hang up and report the calls and the requests to your real IT security team
Ask for their employee ID or badge number, and approve the request if it checks out
Approve it, but change your password straight away once the call is over
questions.explanation: This combines two attack techniques: push bombing followed by a pretexting phone call to social-engineer the victim into approving anyway. Real IT departments don't call asking you to approve suspicious logins; they'd instead help you lock down the account. Hang up and report the entire sequence through a known, verified IT contact.

questions.prompt: You receive an email that looks like a LinkedIn notification: 'A recruiter viewed your profile and left you a message.' The button links to 'linkedin-messages-secure.com'.
options: Click it, since LinkedIn sends these all the time and a recruiter message could matter
Skip the button, type linkedin.com into your browser, and check your messages there
Forward it to your personal email first, so any risk stays off your work computer
Click to see the message, but don't enter your password if a login page pops up
questions.explanation: The real LinkedIn domain is linkedin.com. A lookalike domain like this is a common phishing tactic that preys on professional curiosity (who doesn't want to see who's interested in them?). Always navigate to the real site directly instead of trusting a link, regardless of how legitimate the notification style looks.

questions.prompt: An email appearing to be from your company's IT department says a 'mandatory security training' must be completed by end of day via an external link, or your account will be suspended.
options: Complete it right away, since having your account suspended would cost you a full day
Forward it to the whole team or your manager, because nobody wants to get locked out
Ask IT through the help desk portal or chat so you know it's real before using the link
Leave it until tomorrow, since IT can't reasonably expect training done the same day
questions.explanation: Artificial urgency (a suspension threat) combined with an external link for something that should normally go through internal systems is a classic phishing pattern. Legitimate mandatory training is usually announced through known internal channels in advance, not sprung as an urgent external link.

questions.prompt: You get an email with a PDF attachment named 'Invoice_Overdue_Final_Notice.pdf' from a company you don't recognize, with no other context in the email body.
options: Don't open it; report it and delete it, since you've never done business with them
Open it to see which invoice it is, since a PDF can't do much harm on its own
Open it in a different PDF viewer than usual, so any tricks aimed at yours won't work
Reply and ask which company this is, so you can tell whether it's a real bill
questions.explanation: Unsolicited invoices from unknown senders are a common way to deliver malware through malicious PDF attachments (which can contain embedded scripts or exploit PDF reader vulnerabilities). Since you have no business relationship with the sender, there's no legitimate reason to open it. Report and delete instead.

questions.prompt: A well-formatted email claims to be a job offer from a company you applied to weeks ago, asking you to 'confirm your details' including your SSN and bank info to 'set up payroll' before an interview has even happened.
options: Say no, then call the company on the number listed on its official website
Send the details, since payroll needs them eventually and the email looks professional
Send your SSN but hold back your bank info until after you've had the interview
Reply asking them to call you first, and share the details once you're on the phone
questions.explanation: Legitimate employers only need banking and SSN details after a signed offer and often during onboarding paperwork, never before an interview has even occurred. This is a common 'job offer scam' pattern designed to harvest identity information. Always verify independently through the company's official contact information.

questions.prompt: You receive a calendar invite from an unfamiliar sender titled 'Re: Budget Review' with no message body, just a link labeled 'Join Meeting'.
options: Accept it and join at the meeting time, since budget reviews are normal work meetings
Reply to the invite and ask the organizer what the meeting is about before accepting
Forward it to your manager, since budget meetings are usually their call to accept
Decline or ignore it and leave the link alone, since you don't know who sent it
questions.explanation: Unsolicited calendar invites with vague titles and unfamiliar senders are increasingly used to deliver phishing links, since calendar apps often auto-add these invites and make the link feel more 'official.' Treat an unexpected meeting invite the same as any other unsolicited link, and don't click without verifying.

questions.prompt: An email appears to come from a well-known cloud storage service saying 'Someone shared a document with you.' Hovering over the link shows it actually points to a completely unrelated domain.
options: Click it anyway, since the email design matches that service exactly, logo and all
Copy the link and paste it into a new tab, so you aren't clicking through the email
Reply to the email and ask the sender who shared the document with you and why
Leave it alone, since the real link going somewhere else is a major red flag
questions.explanation: Hovering over a link to preview its real destination is one of the most reliable ways to catch phishing, and a mismatch between what's displayed and where it actually goes is a definitive red flag regardless of how polished the email looks. Copying and pasting the link doesn't help, since it still leads to the same malicious destination.

questions.prompt: You get a phishing-awareness training reminder... except it's real this time, sent by your actual IT department through the normal internal system. How should you treat routine, verified security emails like this?
options: Ignore all security emails on principle, since so many phishing emails use that theme
Engage normally, since it came through the usual system with no pressure tactics
Report it as phishing anyway, since being overly cautious never really hurts anyone
Only read it after a coworker confirms it's real, just to have a second opinion first
questions.explanation: The goal isn't to distrust everything indiscriminately. It's to evaluate each message on its actual indicators (sender legitimacy, urgency tactics, link mismatches, unusual requests). A message from a verified internal system with no red flags is safe to engage with normally; blanket distrust of every security-themed email isn't practical or accurate.

questions.prompt: You get a call from a number matching your company's real main line, with a caller claiming to be from payroll, asking you to confirm your direct deposit account number 'due to a system migration.'
options: Confirm it, since the caller ID shows the company's real main line and not a stranger
Give only the last 4 digits, since that's usually all payroll needs to match it up
Ask them to text you a confirmation code first, so you know it's coming from payroll
Decline, then reach payroll only through a phone number or email address you already have
questions.explanation: Caller ID can be spoofed to display any number, including a real company's main line, so it is not proof of who is actually calling. Payroll or banking detail changes should always be verified through a separate, independently-confirmed channel, never based on trusting the incoming call itself.

questions.prompt: A caller claiming to be from your mobile carrier says your SIM card needs to be 'reactivated' due to suspicious activity, and asks you to read back a verification code that was just texted to you.
options: Read the code back, since it's about protecting your account from suspicious activity
Refuse and hang up, since that code could let someone move your number onto their own SIM
Read out half of the code, so they can start the process without getting all of it
Ask for their employee badge number first, then read the code if they give you one
questions.explanation: This is a classic 'SIM swap' social engineering attempt. The code is what actually lets an attacker transfer your phone number to their own device, which then lets them intercept your other accounts' verification texts. No legitimate carrier support call needs you to read back a verification code.

questions.prompt: You receive a call from someone claiming to represent a well-known software company, saying they detected a virus on your computer through 'routine monitoring' and want remote access to fix it.
options: Let them connect, since they already know about the virus and seem to know the fix
Check which antivirus tool found it, and let them in if the answer sounds legitimate
Hang up, since real software companies don't call you about a virus on your own device
Allow limited access so they can show you the virus without changing any settings
questions.explanation: No legitimate software company monitors your personal computer and calls you unprompted about problems. This is a long-running scam technique ('tech support scam') designed to gain remote access for installing malware or stealing information. Any unsolicited call offering to 'fix' a device problem you didn't report is a red flag.

questions.prompt: A caller claiming to be a company recruiter offers you a work-from-home job with unusually high pay, asks few real questions about your experience, and requests your bank details 'to set up direct deposit for signing bonus' before any formal offer.
options: Share the bank details, since the bonus is paid by direct deposit and that's normal
Say no, since real employers don't ask for bank details before a signed offer
Ask them to send half the bonus upfront first, to prove the job offer is genuine
Give them a secondary bank account, so your main savings are never put at risk
questions.explanation: Unusually high pay for minimal qualification checks, combined with an early request for banking details, matches a common 'job scam' pattern used to either commit fraud or launder money through unwitting participants. Legitimate hiring processes don't ask for financial details this early.

questions.prompt: Someone calls claiming to be from the IRS (or your country's tax authority), saying you owe back taxes and must pay immediately via gift cards or wire transfer or face arrest.
options: Pay right away with the gift cards, since an arrest would be far worse than the cost
Negotiate a payment plan with them over the phone, so the amount is manageable
Ask to speak with a supervisor or manager first, and pay only if they confirm it
Hang up, since tax agencies don't demand gift cards or threaten arrest by phone
questions.explanation: Real tax agencies communicate through official mail first and never demand immediate payment via gift cards, wire transfers, or cryptocurrency, nor do they threaten immediate arrest over the phone. This is one of the most common and well-documented vishing scams; hang up and independently contact the agency through its official number if you have any doubt.

questions.prompt: A caller says they're conducting a 'security audit' on behalf of your company's leadership and asks you to verbally confirm your network login username and password for 'compliance verification.'
options: Refuse, because no real audit would ever need you to say your password out loud
Provide it, because the check comes from leadership and refusing would look uncooperative
Give your username but not your password, since usernames aren't really secret
Ask for a written audit request first, and give the password once it arrives
questions.explanation: No legitimate security audit, compliance process, or IT procedure ever requires an employee to speak their password aloud to another person. Passwords should never be shared under any circumstance, audit-related or otherwise. This is a direct credential-theft attempt dressed up in official-sounding language.

questions.prompt: After you correctly hang up on a suspicious caller, you get a text minutes later from the same number saying 'Sorry we got disconnected, please call us back at this number to finish verifying your account.'
options: Call the number back, since they apologized and the text mentions your account
Text back and ask for a different number, so you're not calling the same caller
Call back, but hang up right away if anything about the call feels suspicious
Ignore it, since calling back just connects you to the same person in a different way
questions.explanation: This is a follow-up manipulation tactic exploiting the fact that you already hung up once and might feel a false sense of resolution or guilt. Calling any number the attacker provides, by phone or text, simply reconnects you to them. If you want to verify anything, look up the organization's real number independently.

questions.prompt: You get a text saying 'Your Netflix payment failed. Update your billing info: [link]', but you don't recognize the phone number and the link isn't Netflix's actual domain.
options: Ignore it, and if you're worried, open the Netflix app directly to check your billing
Tap the link and update your card, so you don't lose access in the middle of a show
Reply to ask which card failed, or which account it is, before you go and update anything
Forward it to Netflix's support number so they can look into it and advise you
questions.explanation: Streaming/subscription billing failures are a very common smishing lure because almost everyone has at least one active subscription. Always check account status by going directly to the real app or website, never through a texted link, especially from an unrecognized number.

questions.prompt: A text claims to be a 'delivery driver' saying they're outside your house and need you to click a link to 'confirm gate code access' since they can't reach the address.
options: Don't tap it; contact the delivery company in its official app to sort out access
Tap the link, because you might actually be expecting a package or a food delivery today
Text your gate code straight back, so the driver can get in without needing a link
Ignore it completely, even though you are actually expecting a package today
questions.explanation: Legitimate delivery services have in-app or direct-call methods for delivery issues; they don't typically text random links asking you to 'confirm access' through an unfamiliar page. If you are expecting a delivery, verify through the official delivery company's own app or number, not a link in an unsolicited text.

questions.prompt: You receive a text: 'You've won a $500 gift card from [Store]! Claim here: [link]' even though you don't recall entering any contest.
options: Tap it to check, since a $500 gift card is worth a quick look even if it's a long shot
Tap it to see the offer, but don't enter any personal or payment details on the page
Delete it, since you can't win a prize from a contest you never actually entered
Reply STOP to unsubscribe first, so they know to remove your number from the list
questions.explanation: You cannot win a contest you never entered. This is one of the oldest scam patterns adapted to text messaging, designed to harvest personal information or install malware through the 'claim' link. There's no safe way to interact with this message; deletion is the correct response.

questions.prompt: A text appears to be from your bank's fraud alert system: 'Suspicious $850 charge detected. Reply YES to confirm this was you, or NO to dispute.' You didn't make this charge.
options: Reply NO right away, so the bank blocks the charge before any more money goes out
Don't reply; call your bank on the number printed on the back of your card
Reply YES to make the alerts stop, then check your statement later to be sure
Forward the text to a friend and ask what they would do before you reply to it
questions.explanation: While some real banks do use text alerts like this, replying either way to a text you can't verify confirms your number is active and engaging with a potential scammer. The safest response is to independently call the number on the back of your actual card, not reply to the text or use any number/link it provides.

questions.prompt: You get a text with a QR code image attached, claiming to be from your apartment complex about a 'new resident portal' you need to set up by scanning it.
options: Scan it right away, since the complex does send resident updates from time to time
Don't scan it; ask the leasing office by phone or in person so you know it's real
Scan it to see the page, but close it immediately without entering any details
Forward the text to other residents to see if they got the same QR code too
questions.explanation: QR codes hide their destination until scanned, making them an effective phishing delivery method ('quishing') via text as well as print. An unexpected request tied to something as sensitive as a 'resident portal' (which likely involves personal/payment info) should always be verified directly with the organization first.

questions.prompt: A text claims to be a two-factor authentication code for an account, but you never requested a login and don't recognize the service name mentioned.
options: Ignore it completely, since you didn't request a code and nothing actually happened
Reply to the text and ask who is trying to log in to the account and why
Take it seriously: check whether that account exists and change its password
Block the number or report it as spam and move on, since that stops more codes arriving
questions.explanation: An unrequested 2FA code, even from an unfamiliar-sounding service, can indicate someone has your email/password for that account and is actively attempting to log in. If you can identify and access that account, changing its password immediately is the safer response than simply ignoring it.

questions.prompt: You get a text that appears to be an automated appointment reminder from a real business you use, with a link to 'reschedule or cancel.' The phone number matches previous legitimate texts from this business.
options: Treat it as suspicious anyway and never tap a texted link, no matter who sent it
Tapping is reasonable, but check the link's destination and what the page asks for
Decline to tap it unless the business also calls you to confirm the appointment
Trust it fully, because appointment reminders or confirmations are always safe to use
questions.explanation: A consistent, previously-verified sending number for a routine, low-stakes action (rescheduling an appointment) is a much lower-risk scenario than an urgent financial or credential request, but it's still good practice to check where a link actually leads before entering any information, since sender spoofing is possible even for known numbers.

questions.prompt: Someone emails claiming to be a new IT vendor performing a 'network inventory' and asks for a list of all employee laptop serial numbers and installed software versions.
options: Send the list, since inventory audits are a normal part of what IT vendors do
Send a partial list first to test their response, or ask for a quote before sending more
Confirm with your IT or procurement team that this vendor and request are real first
Ask them to submit the request through the web form on the company site instead
questions.explanation: Detailed technical inventory information (serial numbers, software versions) is valuable reconnaissance for planning a targeted attack, and 'new vendor doing an audit' is a very plausible-sounding pretext. Any request for this kind of information should be verified with your own IT/procurement team, who would know about a legitimate vendor engagement.

questions.prompt: A person claiming to be a job candidate's reference calls asking detailed questions about a former coworker's salary, performance reviews, and reason for leaving, but you never verified this person is actually conducting a reference check.
options: Answer the questions, since reference checks are a normal part of hiring
Answer only the salary question, since that part seems fairly harmless
Answer now, then ask the former coworker afterward if the call was legitimate
Politely decline and point them to HR's official reference-check process
questions.explanation: Attackers sometimes pose as reference-checkers to extract personal and organizational details about current or former employees. Legitimate reference checks should go through your company's official HR process, which typically requires consent forms and verified requester identity. Informal phone questions bypass all of that.

questions.prompt: Someone calls claiming to be from your company's insurance broker, saying they need to 'verify' the company's EIN (tax ID) and banking details for an 'annual policy renewal.'
options: Provide the details, since annual renewals really do need this kind of paperwork
Hold off, and confirm with finance and your usual broker contact before sharing
Give them the EIN but not the banking details, since the EIN is fairly public anyway
Ask them to email the request in writing first, then provide the details after that
questions.explanation: Company financial identifiers like an EIN combined with banking details are exactly what's needed to commit business fraud or redirect payments. Legitimate renewal processes go through established relationships and internal finance approval, and an inbound call alone should never be sufficient to release this kind of information.

questions.prompt: An email claims to be from a 'law firm' representing a client in a legal dispute with your company, urgently requesting internal emails and documents be sent directly to them 'before a filing deadline.'
options: Send the documents quickly, so the company doesn't miss the court's filing deadline
Ask a coworker or your team lead if they've heard of the law firm, then send the files
Forward the request to your legal department and let them verify and respond
Send only the documents that look non-sensitive, so you partly meet the deadline
questions.explanation: Legal requests for internal documents should always be routed through your own legal department, which can verify the requester's legitimacy and ensure documents are handled appropriately (including under privilege or confidentiality rules). An employee unilaterally sending internal documents based on an urgent-sounding email is exactly what this pretext is designed to produce.

questions.prompt: A caller claims to be a 'building inspector' following up on a mentioned fire code issue, asking to be let into server/equipment rooms without a scheduled appointment or visible ID.
options: Ask for proof of an appointment and ID, and confirm with building management first
Let them in, because fire code problems can be dangerous or even shut the building down
Let them in, but stay with them the whole time so they can't do anything unusual
Ask a coworker to escort them around, so the inspection can be finished sooner
questions.explanation: Legitimate inspections are typically scheduled in advance and inspectors carry verifiable identification. An unscheduled visit requesting access to sensitive areas (server rooms) should be verified with building management or the relevant authority before granting any access, regardless of how official the reason sounds.

questions.prompt: Someone messages you on a professional networking site claiming to be a 'former colleague' from a company you worked at years ago, quickly steering the conversation toward asking about your current employer's internal tools and security software.
options: Avoid sharing security details, and confirm who they are by asking a mutual contact
Answer their questions, since catching up with old colleagues is perfectly normal
Answer only if their profile picture or job history looks familiar from your time there
Block them immediately and report nothing, since that ends the conversation fast
questions.explanation: Fabricated 'former colleague' profiles are a known reconnaissance tactic, especially when a conversation quickly pivots toward extracting details about your current employer's security posture. Casual reconnection is fine, but specific technical questions about internal tools warrant caution and independent verification.

questions.prompt: A pretexting attempt fails because an employee simply says: 'I can't share that, but I'm happy to have my manager follow up with you directly.' What made this response effective?
options: It was blunt enough that the attacker decided the target wasn't worth the effort
It bought time by promising a follow-up, so the attacker would eventually give up
It shared nothing and moved the request to a proper channel that can verify it
It worked mainly because the employee sounded confident or firm enough on the call
questions.explanation: An effective response to a suspected pretexting attempt neither confirms nor denies any sensitive details (which itself can leak information) and redirects the interaction to a verifiable, proper channel. Confidence and tone matter less than simply not engaging with the substance of the request until legitimacy is established.

questions.prompt: You're exiting a secure building just as someone else is trying to enter behind you without badging in. They smile and say 'thanks!' as they walk through the door you're holding open on your way out.
options: Let the door close and ask them to badge in, even if you're just on your way out
Let it go, since you were leaving anyway and weren't really letting anyone in
Hold it open, since refusing someone who just thanked you would feel awkward
Only worry about tailgating when you're entering, because that's when it really matters
questions.explanation: Tailgating works the same way regardless of which direction you're moving through the door. If an unauthorized person gets inside because you held the door, the security control has been bypassed either way. The correct habit is letting secure doors close fully behind you regardless of your own direction of travel.

questions.prompt: A person wearing a lanyard from a well-known partner company asks to be let into a restricted meeting room area, saying they have a meeting with someone who 'should be here any minute.'
options: Let them in and wait with them, or find them a seat, until their contact finally arrives
Let them in, since a badge from a well-known partner company seems legit enough
Ask them to call their contact from the hallway, then let them in once they have
Ask them to wait at reception until their contact can come and get them in person
questions.explanation: A partner company's badge doesn't grant them access rights to your restricted areas. Visitors should always be received and escorted by their actual host, not let in based on a plausible story while waiting for someone to 'maybe' show up. Directing them to reception maintains the access control properly.

questions.prompt: You notice someone struggling to open a badge-access door using what looks like an expired or clearly damaged badge, asking if you can let them in since 'the system is being weird.'
options: Send them to building security or the front desk to get the badge issue sorted out
Let them in, because a glitchy badge reader or expired card sounds like a real tech problem
Swipe your own badge for them a few times, since it might just need a retry
Let them in, then mention the broken badge to security later so it gets fixed
questions.explanation: A badge that doesn't work should be resolved through the proper channel (security/front desk), not bypassed by someone else's badge. Using your own credentials to let someone else through defeats the entire point of individual access tracking, even when the excuse sounds technical and plausible.

questions.prompt: During a fire drill, everyone exits together through an emergency door that's propped open. Afterward, people start filtering back in through that same still-propped door instead of the main badge entrance.
options: Close and secure the propped door, and have everyone come back in through badge access
Leave it, because everyone is just getting back to work and it will swing shut eventually
Keep it propped for the rest of the day, since there might be another drill later
Only worry about the propped door if you see a stranger actually trying to use it
questions.explanation: Emergency exits propped open during a drill create a real window of vulnerability if left that way afterward, since anyone, not just employees, could walk in unnoticed during the chaos of people filtering back. Doors should be restored to their normal secured state as soon as the drill situation ends.

questions.prompt: A group of several people badge through a secure door together, and only the first person actually scans their badge while the rest just walk through behind them quickly.
options: It's fine, since it's faster and they're almost certainly coworkers or contractors
It's only a real problem if more than five people walk through on one badge
It's fine as long as the first and last person in the group both badge in
Each person should badge in on their own, even if it slows the group down
questions.explanation: Groups walking through on one badge scan is a very common, often unintentional form of tailgating. It feels efficient and harmless, especially among people who look like they belong, but it defeats individual access logging and control entirely. The habit of each person badging in separately should hold regardless of group size or familiarity.

questions.prompt: Someone claiming to be a new employee who 'hasn't gotten their badge yet' asks to follow you into a secure area on their first day, mentioning their manager's name to sound credible.
options: Let them in, since new employees really do wait a few days for their badges
Let them in and introduce them around, so people know they're new on the team
Send them to reception or HR so they can check in and get a temporary badge or escort
Ask them to text their manager, and let them in if the reply looks right
questions.explanation: Genuine new employees without a badge yet should be processed through reception/HR, which can issue a temporary badge or provide a verified escort, and this exact scenario ('new, badge pending, knows a name') is also a very common tailgating pretext. Directing them to the proper process protects against both possibilities without seeming distrustful.

questions.prompt: What's the most effective general habit for preventing tailgating, regardless of the specific excuse someone gives?
options: Memorizing every coworker's face, so you can spot a stranger the moment you see one
Making sure doors latch behind you, and sending anyone without their own badge to reception
Watching for tailgating during business hours, since that's when most people come in
Trusting people who seem calm and confident, since attackers tend to act nervous
questions.explanation: No one can realistically memorize every coworker's face at a mid-to-large organization, and confidence/rushing aren't reliable indicators of legitimacy, and attackers exploit exactly those assumptions. The one habit that works regardless of the excuse is simply ensuring secure doors close behind you and redirecting anyone without their own access to the proper check-in process.

questions.prompt: You receive an email from your 'CEO's assistant' asking you to purchase software licenses using your personal credit card, promising reimbursement, since the CEO is 'traveling and can't approve a normal purchase order right now.'
options: Buy it and expense it later, because the CEO's office wouldn't ask unless it were really needed
Buy a smaller amount on your card to limit your own risk if something goes wrong
Decline, and follow the normal purchasing process however urgent it's made to sound
Ask a coworker to buy it on their card instead, so it's not your money at stake
questions.explanation: Asking an employee to use personal funds and bypass normal purchasing/approval processes is a strong BEC red flag, since legitimate urgent situations still have proper emergency purchasing procedures. 'Traveling and can't approve normally' is a convenient excuse attackers use to justify skipping verification steps.

questions.prompt: An email from what looks like your company's actual domain (correctly spelled, matching signature) asks you to change the payroll direct deposit account for another employee 'per their request over the phone.'
options: Make the change, since the email comes from the real company domain and signature
Talk to the employee in person or by phone so you know it's really their request
Make the change, but flag it so it gets looked at in the next monthly audit
Decline for now and ask the sender for the employee's phone number as proof first
questions.explanation: Even a correct-looking domain can result from a genuinely compromised email account, not just a spoofed one, so domain legitimacy alone isn't sufficient verification for a payroll change. Any request to redirect someone else's pay should be confirmed directly with that actual employee before action is taken.

questions.prompt: You get an urgent message that appears to be from your manager on a messaging app, asking you to purchase several hundred dollars in gift cards for a 'team appreciation surprise' and to keep it confidential from the team until the reveal.
options: Buy the gift cards and keep it quiet, since spoiling the surprise would be awkward
Talk to your manager in person first, especially given the request for secrecy
Buy a smaller amount now and ask for reimbursement once the reveal is done
Ask another coworker to split the cost with you, so it's less money up front
questions.explanation: Requests combining gift cards, urgency, and secrecy ('don't tell the team yet') are a textbook BEC pattern, and the secrecy instruction specifically discourages you from casually verifying with others who might recognize it as suspicious. Verify directly with your manager through a known channel before purchasing anything, regardless of how normal the stated reason sounds.

questions.prompt: An email thread that appears to be a real, ongoing conversation between your company and a known vendor suddenly includes a new message asking to redirect an upcoming payment to a 'temporary new account' due to a banking issue on the vendor's side.
options: Call the vendor on a number you already had on file and confirm before paying
Pay the new account, since the request came in the same thread you've been using
Split the payment between the old and new accounts, or pay a small test amount first
Reply in the same thread and ask the vendor to confirm the new account details
questions.explanation: Attackers sometimes compromise one party's email and quietly insert themselves into legitimate, ongoing email threads, making the request look highly credible since it fits the existing conversation. This is exactly why verification must happen through a separate channel (a phone call to a previously known number), not by asking again within the same potentially compromised thread.

questions.prompt: Your company's finance team receives an email claiming to be from a law firm handling a confidential acquisition, instructing an urgent wire transfer to 'finalize the deal' and stressing that discussing it with anyone else would violate a non-disclosure agreement.
options: Escalate it up the normal chain of command, whatever the NDA supposedly says
Process the wire, because NDAs really are common in confidential acquisitions or mergers
Send a partial payment to show good faith while you check whether it's real
Ask the law firm to send more documentation over the same email to prove it
questions.explanation: This is a well-documented BEC variant ('CEO fraud' combined with fake M&A urgency) that uses confidentiality and legal-sounding pressure specifically to prevent the target from checking with anyone who might recognize the scam. Legitimate high-value transactions still go through internal approval chains, and a claimed NDA doesn't override that.

questions.prompt: You notice the 'reply-to' address on an email from your 'CFO' is subtly different from their actual email address, even though the 'from' name displayed looks correct.
options: Ignore it, since the display name is correct and that's what most people check
Reply anyway, but ask a clarifying question first to see how they respond
Only worry about it if the request in the email also seems unusual somehow
Treat it as a serious red flag, since a mismatched reply-to is a common spoofing sign
questions.explanation: A mismatched reply-to address is one of the more reliable technical indicators of email spoofing, since attackers can freely set a display name but the reply-to reveals where responses actually go. This should be treated as a serious warning sign on its own, not something to only notice if the content also seems suspicious.

questions.prompt: What is the single most reliable defense against BEC scams, regardless of how convincing the email, sender name, or urgency appears?
options: Checking whether the email has good grammar, spelling, or formatting before acting on it
Trusting emails that come from recognized internal domains and known senders
Confirming any money or data request through a separate channel you already trust
Waiting 24 hours before acting on any email, so the urgency has time to fade
questions.explanation: Grammar quality, sender domain, and even waiting periods can all be worked around or don't reliably indicate legitimacy, since modern BEC attacks are often well-written and can come from genuinely compromised accounts. Independent, separate-channel verification (a phone call to a known number, an in-person check) is the one defense that consistently works regardless of how convincing the email itself is.

questions.prompt: You receive a free promotional USB fan at a job fair from a company booth. It's branded and looks professionally made.
options: Power it from a wall outlet or a USB data blocker instead of a laptop's data port
Plug it into your laptop, since it came from a legitimate company's booth at the fair
Plug it into a public charging station instead, so your own devices stay safe
Assume it's safe to plug in anywhere, since it's just a fan and not a storage device
questions.explanation: Even 'just a fan' can carry hidden data/firmware risks depending on manufacturing supply chain integrity, and any USB device plugged into a data port could theoretically carry malicious firmware. Using a wall outlet or a data-blocker avoids exposing your computer's data lines regardless of what the device claims to be.

questions.prompt: A QR code sticker on a parking meter says 'Scan to pay for parking' but looks slightly different from the meter's other official stickers: different font, slightly askew placement.
options: Don't scan it; pay through the city's official parking app or at the meter instead
Scan it, since it's still probably the real payment system with a new sticker
Scan it, but back out before paying if the page or the web address looks at all strange
Peel it off to see if there's another sticker underneath, and scan that one
questions.explanation: Attackers have physically placed fraudulent QR code stickers over legitimate ones on parking meters and public signage in real documented incidents, leading victims to fake payment pages that steal card details. Visual inconsistencies (font, placement) are a valid reason for suspicion. Use the official app or another verified payment method instead.

questions.prompt: You find a USB drive in a company breakroom with a sticky note that says 'HR - Confidential Layoff List - DO NOT SHARE'.
options: Plug it in privately to check whether you or your coworkers are on the list
Ask around the office or in the team chat whether anyone lost it, to get it back to them
Take it straight to HR, since it's their file, without mentioning it to IT
Hand it to the security team without plugging it in, however tempting the label is
questions.explanation: This label is specifically engineered to exploit curiosity and workplace anxiety, making it more tempting than a generic file name would be, and that's exactly what makes it a more dangerous USB drop attack. The correct response doesn't change based on how compelling the label is: hand it to IT/security without connecting it to anything.

questions.prompt: You want to charge your phone quickly and the only available option is a USB charging cable at a public airport charging kiosk (not a wall plug).
options: Use it, since the airport provides it for travelers and maintains the kiosks
Use your own wall charger or a USB data blocker rather than the kiosk's cable
Use it, but only for a few minutes or until it's at 20% to limit how long it's exposed
Use it only if your phone is almost dead, since that's worth the small risk
questions.explanation: Public USB charging kiosks are a known vector for 'juice jacking,' where a compromised cable/port can access data or install malware while charging. Bringing your own wall adapter (which only draws power, not data) or a USB data-blocker avoids the risk entirely, and this holds true regardless of how low your battery is.

questions.prompt: A colleague from another department hands you a USB drive at a work event saying 'here's that presentation I mentioned', but you don't actually recall having that conversation.
options: Plug it in, because they seem to know you and you're at an official work event anyway
Plug it into a personal device first, so your work laptop is never exposed
Take it and plug it in later, since asking more questions would feel awkward
Politely ask them to email the file, or talk it through before using the drive
questions.explanation: Physical social engineering can involve genuinely misidentifying someone or using a vague, plausible-sounding pretext ('that presentation') to get a device connected. Asking for the file over email instead, or clarifying the context first, sidesteps the risk without necessarily accusing anyone of bad intent.

questions.prompt: Your company issues a policy that all USB ports on work laptops are disabled by default, requiring an IT request to enable them for a specific, approved reason. A coworker complains this is 'overkill.'
options: Agree that it's excessive, since USB drives are such a convenient way to work
Suggest people just be careful with USB drives, since that's simpler for everyone
See it as a reasonable, common control, given how often USB attacks succeed
Support it only for shared or public computers, since work laptops are lower risk
questions.explanation: Disabling USB ports by default is a well-established security control precisely because USB-based attacks (drops, baited devices, juice jacking) are common and effective even against otherwise careful, well-trained employees. 'Being careful' alone hasn't proven sufficient at scale, which is why technical controls like this exist as a backstop.

questions.prompt: What's the underlying reason USB drop attacks and malicious QR codes tend to work, even on people who intellectually know the risk?
options: People are generally careless about security and don't think before acting
They play on curiosity and convenience, which can override caution in the moment
Most computers have no protection at all against USB devices plugged into them
These attacks mostly work on brand-new or non-technical staff who don't know any better
questions.explanation: These attacks are effective specifically because they're engineered around natural human curiosity and the convenience of scanning/plugging something in, not because people are careless or unintelligent. Even security-aware people can be caught off guard in a moment of curiosity, which is why habitual caution (not just knowledge) matters.

questions.prompt: You receive a voicemail that sounds exactly like your company's HR director, asking you to call back a number to 'confirm some employment details', but the callback number isn't one you recognize as HR's actual line.
options: Call back the number given, since the voice sounded exactly like the HR director
Look up HR's real phone number in the company directory and call that instead
Check by texting the number first, then call back once they confirm it's HR
Delete the voicemail and do nothing, since it's probably nothing important
questions.explanation: A convincing voice, even an AI-cloned one, doesn't verify the callback number provided is legitimate, since attackers rely on you calling the number they gave rather than one you already know is real. Always use an independently known contact number rather than one provided within the suspicious message itself.

questions.prompt: During a live phone call that sounds exactly like a close friend in urgent distress asking for money, you notice the request is oddly generic and they avoid answering a specific personal question naturally.
options: Trust the call, since the voice sounds exactly like your friend and they're upset
Send a small amount of money for now, so they're not stuck while you figure it out
Treat the vague answers as a red flag, and reach your friend another way you already know
Ask them to send a photo to prove it's them, and send the money once it arrives
questions.explanation: Even highly convincing voice cloning can struggle with truly spontaneous, specific personal knowledge in real-time conversation, and noticing that gap is a valid signal. A photo can also be manipulated or reused, so the safest verification is independently reaching them through a different channel or number you already know is theirs.

questions.prompt: Your company adopts a policy requiring a secondary verification method (like a pre-agreed code word) for any phone-based request involving money or sensitive data, specifically because of AI voice cloning risks. A colleague says this feels 'paranoid.'
options: Agree that it's excessive, because these attacks are probably very rare or only hit big firms
Support it only for executives, since they're the ones attackers actually target
Suggest checking caller ID instead, since it's simpler and nearly as effective
See it as a reasonable, low-effort safeguard, given how good voice cloning has become
questions.explanation: Voice cloning tools have become widely accessible and require only seconds of sample audio, making this a genuinely current risk rather than a rare edge case, and caller ID is trivially spoofable so it offers no real protection. A pre-agreed verification method (code word, callback protocol) is a low-effort, high-value safeguard worth having regardless of how 'paranoid' it might feel.

questions.prompt: You get a voicemail, again sounding like your CEO, this time simply thanking the team for their hard work this quarter, with no requests, no urgency, nothing actionable.
options: Treat it with the same suspicion as any other CEO voice message, whatever it actually says
Report it to IT security immediately, just in case the voice is a cloned fake
Assume any message mentioning the CEO has to be verified through a formal process
Take it at face value, since the real risk is in requests for money, data, or access
questions.explanation: The actual danger from voice cloning comes from its use to manipulate someone into an action (sending money, sharing credentials, granting access). A message with no request or urgency, even if theoretically fake, poses no real risk. Applying the same intense scrutiny to every single voice message regardless of content isn't practical or necessary; the focus should be on messages that ask you to do something.

questions.prompt: On a video call, you notice slight lag or unnatural mouth movement mismatches with the audio from someone requesting an urgent, unusual action.
options: Treat the glitches plus the urgent request as a reason to verify another way first
Ignore the glitches, because video calls often lag or freeze and it's probably their Wi-Fi
Ask them to turn off their camera, and see whether the audio still sounds right
Carry on with the call, but mention the lag out loud so they know you noticed
questions.explanation: While video call glitches are common and often harmless on their own, combined with an unusual or urgent request they become a meaningful signal worth acting on. Turning the camera off would actually remove the one clue (visual mismatch) that could help you catch a deepfake, so that's the wrong move; independent verification through another channel is the safer choice.

questions.prompt: A scammer would need what, at minimum, to create a convincing AI clone of someone's voice using current widely-available tools?
options: Years of audio engineering experience and expensive professional studio equipment
Physical access to the target's phone, so they can record calls from the device
Just a few seconds of the person's voice, taken from a public video they posted online
Help from the target's phone carrier, since that's where call recordings are kept
questions.explanation: Modern voice cloning tools can produce convincing results from just a few seconds of publicly available audio, with no special training, physical device access, or carrier involvement is required. This low barrier is exactly why the threat has become significant enough for regular employees and individuals to need awareness of it, not just high-profile targets.

questions.prompt: What is the most reliable single defense against AI voice/video impersonation for sensitive requests?
options: Listening very closely for subtle glitches or robotic sounds in the caller's voice
Only accepting sensitive requests over video, because video is much harder or impossible to fake
Asking the caller to state their full name, job title, and employee ID number
Confirming the request through a separate channel you trust, however real it sounds
questions.explanation: Voice/video quality has advanced to the point where 'listening for imperfections' isn't a reliable defense, and asking someone to state their name proves nothing since the attacker already knows who they're impersonating. Independent, separate-channel verification remains the one method that works regardless of how technically convincing the impersonation is.

questions.prompt: You're at a coffee shop working on a sensitive document, and someone sits at a nearby table with a clear line of sight to your screen.
options: Carry on, because most people in a coffee shop aren't paying attention to other screens
Ask the person to move tables, since you're working on something confidential
Work faster so you can finish the sensitive part before it becomes a problem
Move seats, use a privacy screen, or save sensitive work for somewhere more private
questions.explanation: Shoulder surfing doesn't require malicious intent to be a real risk, since sensitive information can be casually observed and even unintentionally remembered or photographed. Practical steps like repositioning, using a privacy screen, or deferring sensitive work to a more controlled environment are more reliable than hoping no one happens to look.

questions.prompt: You receive a new company laptop and are deciding how to secure it against theft while working in public or shared spaces.
options: Leave it unattended for a moment or two if needed, because laptop theft is relatively rare
Keep it in your bag when you're not using it, with the bag on the floor beside you
Use a cable lock in shared spaces, and never leave it alone in public, even briefly
Rely on the laptop's password lock, since a thief can't get into it without it
questions.explanation: A locked screen protects data but does nothing to prevent the physical device itself from being picked up and walked away with, and 'briefly' is exactly the window opportunistic theft relies on. Physical securing methods (cable locks, never leaving it unattended) address a different risk than password protection and both matter.

questions.prompt: You're setting up for a presentation using a conference room's shared computer, and notice a previous user left their email account still logged in.
options: Log the previous user's account out completely before you start using the machine
Leave it and open a new browser tab or window for your own work, without touching theirs
Take a screenshot of what they left open, and send it to them as a friendly heads-up
Use it as it is, since you're not planning to look through their account anyway
questions.explanation: Leaving someone else's account logged in on a shared machine, even unintentionally, is an active exposure that should be closed as a matter of basic hygiene. Simply not looking through it yourself doesn't protect the previous user, since anyone using the machine afterward could see it. Logging them out (not just ignoring it) is the responsible action.

questions.prompt: Your company's cleaning staff has after-hours access to all office areas as part of their contract. What's a reasonable physical security practice given this?
options: Leave documents out overnight if needed, since the cleaning staff have been vetted
Keep a clean desk anyway, locking away documents and screens whoever has access
Only worry about a clean desk in departments that handle highly classified data
Ask the cleaning staff to skip certain desks or offices, so sensitive papers are left alone
questions.explanation: Even trusted, vetted personnel with legitimate access represent one more point where information could be exposed, misplaced, or seen by someone else who briefly enters that space (a visitor, a substitute cleaner, etc.). A consistent clean-desk practice reduces exposure regardless of how much you trust any specific group with legitimate access.

questions.prompt: You're disposing of an old external hard drive that contained work files, after already copying what you need elsewhere.
options: Have it securely wiped or destroyed through the company's IT asset disposal process
Throw it in the regular trash, since the important files are already copied elsewhere
