Reformat it first, then give it away or sell it, since formatting clears the drive
Peel off the drive's label before throwing it out, so nobody knows it was yours
questions.explanation: A simple reformat or even deleting files often doesn't actually erase the underlying data, which can be recovered with commonly available tools, and removing a label doesn't address this at all. Proper IT asset disposal (secure wiping or physical destruction) is necessary specifically because 'looks empty' and 'is actually empty' are very different things for storage media.

questions.prompt: You're setting a new passcode for your work phone, which has access to company email and internal apps. What's a reasonable minimum standard, physical-security-wise?
options: A simple 4-digit PIN like 1234, because the phone is almost always in your pocket or bag
No passcode at all, since the phone is rarely out of your sight during the day
The same PIN you use for your bank card, so it's easy to remember in a hurry
A longer passcode that's hard to guess, with biometric unlock set up as backup
questions.explanation: A device with access to company email and internal systems is a meaningful target if lost or stolen, so weak/default PINs, no passcode, or reusing a financial PIN all create unnecessary risk. A longer, non-obvious passcode with biometric convenience balances real security with usability.

questions.prompt: What's the underlying principle connecting most physical security practices (locking screens, shredding documents, securing devices, clean desks)?
options: Assuming everyone around you has bad intentions and could be an attacker
Reducing easy chances for information to leak, even when no one means harm
Following the rules mainly so that compliance paperwork and audits stay clean
Protecting classified information, since that's the main case where it matters
questions.explanation: None of these practices require assuming malicious intent from those around you; they simply reduce the everyday, low-effort opportunities where information or access could be casually exposed, misused, or stolen, whether by an opportunistic stranger, a curious visitor, or genuine accident. This principle applies broadly, not just in high-security or classified environments.

questions.prompt: Your company switches from simple 'approve/deny' push notifications to a system requiring you to type in a number shown on your computer screen into your phone app to approve a login. Why is this considered a stronger defense against MFA fatigue?
options: It isn't really different from an approve or deny button, only a bit slower to use
It mostly adds an extra step, so people pay attention a little bit longer
The attacker can't see the number on your real login screen, so spamming fails
It only works when the phone and computer are on the same Wi-Fi network
questions.explanation: Number-matching MFA specifically defeats push-bombing because approving requires seeing and entering a number that only appears on the legitimate login screen, so an attacker spamming requests has no way to make the victim see or know that number, so blind 'approve' taps no longer work the same way. This is a meaningful design difference, not just an extra annoying click.

questions.prompt: You get an MFA push notification while you're in the middle of legitimately trying to log in yourself, but the request shows a login location or device you don't recognize.
options: Approve it, since you are in fact trying to log in right now and it's expected
Approve it so you can get in, and then check the location details afterward
Approve it, since the odd location is probably just a display glitch in the app
Deny it, since your own login attempt doesn't prove this request is yours
questions.explanation: It's possible for an attacker's login attempt to arrive around the same time as your own legitimate one, especially if your password is already compromised, and approving based on timing coincidence alone isn't safe. Always check the location/device details shown in the prompt before approving, even if you are in fact trying to log in.

questions.prompt: After denying a flood of suspicious MFA requests and changing your password, what should you do about your MFA method itself?
options: Reset your MFA device too, and review your account recovery settings as well
Nothing more is needed, because the new password already locks the attacker out for good
Turn MFA off for a while until things calm down, so the prompts stop coming
Ignore any future prompts from now on, since you know they're not really yours
questions.explanation: A determined attacker who had your password might have also attempted other account changes; reviewing and potentially resetting MFA registration and recovery settings closes off additional avenues they might have tried. Turning MFA off entirely would remove your strongest remaining protection at exactly the wrong time.

questions.prompt: A friend says MFA fatigue attacks 'only happen to big companies with lots of employees.' Is that accurate?
options: Yes, since attackers don't bother targeting individual personal accounts this way
Only for executives, since they're the accounts worth the attacker's effort
No, since any account with push MFA can be targeted once the password is known
Only for accounts without a strong password, since those are easy to get into
questions.explanation: MFA fatigue works on any account using push-based approval once an attacker has the underlying password, and it's not limited by organization size, seniority, or even whether it's a personal versus work account. High-profile breaches involving this technique at large companies are simply the ones that made the news, not the limit of where it applies.

questions.prompt: Why does an attacker need your password before an MFA fatigue attack can even begin?
options: They don't, since push requests can be triggered with just your email address
They need it to find out which phone number to send all the push requests to
It isn't really needed, since MFA fatigue attacks work around passwords entirely
The login that triggers the push only starts once the correct password has been entered
questions.explanation: A push notification is triggered by an actual login attempt reaching the MFA step, which requires the correct username and password to get that far in the first place. This is also exactly why an unexpected MFA prompt is itself proof of a compromised password, even before you approve or deny anything.

questions.prompt: Your IT department sends a company-wide reminder: 'Never approve an MFA request you did not personally initiate, no matter who asks you to.' A coworker asks why this needs to be said explicitly.
options: It doesn't really need saying, since it's obvious to everyone who uses MFA
Attackers pair push floods with pressure, like fake IT calls, to override judgment
It's just standard corporate boilerplate or legal wording that doesn't serve much purpose
It's mainly meant for new employees who haven't used MFA at work or at home before
questions.explanation: The reason this needs explicit reinforcement is that real attacks combine the technical push-bombing with social engineering (a follow-up call pretending to be IT) specifically designed to override people's instinct to deny, and experienced employees have fallen for this exact combination. Stating it plainly and repeatedly helps counteract that social pressure in the moment.

questions.prompt: What's the single most important takeaway about MFA fatigue attacks for any employee?
options: Deny any MFA request you didn't start, no matter who asks, and report it
MFA isn't a very useful security measure, since attackers can get around it
Only worry about it if the requests come more than ten times in a row
It's IT's problem to solve, not something individual employees need to handle
questions.explanation: MFA remains a strong security measure overall, since the attack specifically exploits human response to repeated prompts and social pressure, not a flaw in MFA itself. The core individual takeaway is simple and doesn't depend on volume or persuasion: never approve a request you didn't initiate, and report it immediately when it happens.
